title: Misconduct — Organisational Disciplinary Process Flow
subtitle: Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 and the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294) · As at 19 October 2026

overview.summary: This flow tells an employer what to do, by when, and who hands off to whom, from the moment possible misconduct comes to light until the matter closes and lessons feed back into controls. It follows a generic disciplinary process in this order:

notes.text: The flow assumes no collective agreement or bargaining council procedure applies, and must be adjusted where one does.

notes.heading: Legal status
notes.text: The fairness of a dismissal is governed by the LRA (ss.185, 186(1), 188 and 192). Disciplinary action short of dismissal, including suspension and warnings, is tested as an unfair labour practice under s.186(2)(b). The Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (“the Code”), issued under s.203(2A) of the LRA (GN 3470, GG 53294) and in effect from 4 September 2025, repealed the Schedule 8 Code of Good Practice: Dismissal and the 1999 Code of Good Practice on Operational Requirements. The Code is guidance, not statute, but anyone considering whether a dismissal was for a fair reason or in accordance with a fair procedure must take it into account (s.188(2), s.203(3)). The Code does not deal with precautionary suspension or with the order of proceedings at an enquiry; both are governed by case law and internal policy. A search on 29 September 2026 found no amendment to the Code since publication; status should be re-checked before this flow is adopted.

notes.heading: Labels used throughout
points: LRA = the Labour Relations Act and other statutes; binding now.
Code = the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (cited by item number); must be taken into account, and departures must be justified.
CL = a principle from case law, cited by name, court and year. Verify the citation and any later authority before using it in advice.
BP = best practice or internal control; not a statutory deadline. Adopt as policy so it becomes binding internally.

notes.heading: Design principle
notes.text: Internal targets sit inside every statutory limit, and the clock starts on the day any manager learns of the incident, because unexplained delay weakens both the case and any suspension. The flow screens first and charges second: the label chosen (misconduct, incapacity, poor performance or probation) decides which test applies. The 48-hour minimum for the notice to attend is a floor, not a target: the Code’s test is a reasonable period to prepare (item 11(4)(b)), so complex matters get longer.

notes.heading: Six interpretation points that shape the flow
points: The weight of the Code. The Code is intentionally general and departures “may be justified in proper circumstances” (item 2(1)); it does not alter rights under a collective agreement (item 2(3)); and it must not be read as requiring small businesses to do what is impractical (item 3). A recognition agreement or bargaining council procedure therefore prevails over this flow. The employer may depart from its own rules and procedures if there is a justification (item 6(7)): record that justification at the time.

Counting time. LRA referral periods (30 days for a dismissal, 90 days for an unfair labour practice, s.191(1)(b)) are calendar days under the Interpretation Act 33 of 1957 s.4. The Rules for the Conduct of Proceedings before the CCMA, 2023 (rule 3) count time in calendar days, excluding the first day and including the last; if the last day falls on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday, the period ends on the next working day. The former 16 December to 7 January exclusion no longer applies. Internal steps in this flow use working days. The 48-hour notice period runs from proven service of the notice to the start of the enquiry; as policy, it must include at least two full working days, so a notice served on Friday afternoon does not support a Monday enquiry.

Precautionary suspension is not a sanction. The Constitutional Court has held that a precautionary suspension is not disciplinary action; its fairness turns on whether there is a fair reason, the prejudice to the employee, and whether it is on full pay, and a prior hearing is not a legal requirement (CL: Long v South African Breweries, CC 2019). The Labour Court has nonetheless favoured giving the employee an opportunity to make representations (CL: SAPU v National Commissioner of the SAPS, LC 2005; Mogothle v Premier of the North West Province, LC 2009). Footnote 2 of the Code lists “suspension” among graduated disciplinary measures: that is unpaid suspension as a sanction, a different thing, available only after a fair process and where the code or contract provides for it (verify).

The enquiry is not a criminal trial. The Code requires “a genuine dialogue and an opportunity for reflection” (item 11(1)) and says an enquiry need not be formal (item 11(3)). The adversarial sequence in Phase 4 (opening, evidence in chief, cross-examination, closing) is used because it is the clearest way to give an adequate opportunity to respond where facts are disputed. It should be run fairly and without technicality (CL: Avril Elizabeth Home v CCMA, LC 2006). For admitted or simple matters the chair may shorten it, with reasons.

Misconduct, incapacity or something else. Misconduct is a culpable breach of a rule or standard (items 7 to 10). Poor work performance after probation (items 19–20), ill health and injury (item 21(1)–(5)), incompatibility (item 21(7)) and probation (items 14–18) have their own tests. Dependency on alcohol or drugs may call for counselling and rehabilitation (item 21(4)). An employee on a COIDA claim is handled with the COIDA flow and RRR Regulations reg 10(1)(m)–(n). Action against someone who has made a protected disclosure risks an automatically unfair dismissal (s.187(1)(h)): run the PDA flow in parallel.

Who is the employer, and who is being disciplined. A temporary employment service is the employer of the workers it places (s.198(2)); the client reports the conduct and may ask for removal, but the TES runs the discipline, subject to the deeming provisions for lower-earning placed workers (s.198A: placed workers earning below the BCEA threshold, R269 600.90 p.a. from 1 May 2026, are deemed employees of the client after three months unless the placement is a genuine temporary service). Discipline of a trade union representative or office-bearer should not be instituted without first informing and consulting the union (item 11(7)). Public-service employers follow their bargaining council resolutions, which set their own suspension and hearing time limits.

notes.heading: Roles used
notes.text: Employee Relations Officer (ERO, the case owner; in smaller organisations the HR manager); Line Manager (LM); Investigator (INV); Initiator (INI, the employer party at the enquiry); Chairperson (CHR, independent of the matter); Appeal Chairperson (APC); Legal Adviser (LA); HR Manager (HR); Payroll (PAY); IT and Security (ITS); Senior Sign-off (SSO, e.g. HR Director or COO; the Board chair where an executive is implicated); Board, Remuneration or Social and Ethics Committee (BOARD). The employee (EMP) and their representative (REP: a fellow employee or trade union representative, item 11(4)(c)); together, “the employee party”. External: trade union (TU); CCMA or bargaining council (CCMA/BC); SAPS.

stages.title: Phase 0 — Readiness (standing obligations)
intro: Phase 0 has no case trigger. It must be in place before the first incident, because whether the employee “was aware, or could reasonably be expected to have been aware” of the rule (item 8(2)(b)), and whether the rule was consistently applied (item 8(2)(e)), are fixed by what happened before the conduct.

notes.heading: Employee side of Phase 0
notes.text: Nothing is owed by an employee yet, but the rule-awareness test in item 8(2)(b) is decided here. An employee who was never shown the testing policy is hard to discipline for refusing a test.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A code the chairperson has never read, or that conflicts with a recognition agreement, is a common source of procedural unfairness. Reconcile before adoption.

steps.action: Where HR capacity is limited, adopt a simplified procedure that keeps the core: tell the employee what is alleged, give a reasonable chance to respond on the allegation and the sanction, decide on the evidence, give reasons, keep a record.

stages.title: Phase 1 — Incident and preliminary investigation
intro: Day 0 is the day any supervisor or manager first learns of the possible misconduct. The preliminary investigation answers three questions by working day 5 (BP): is there a case to answer; does the employee’s presence pose a risk that justifies considering suspension; and which route should the matter take. It makes no finding of guilt. The full evidence is gathered in Phase 3.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Follow a lawful instruction to stop work or leave the site; report what happened truthfully; do not delete records or approach witnesses. An employee may decline to give a statement, but should be told the process may continue on the evidence available.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: LM → ERO (same day). ERO → ITS (evidence and access). ERO → LA (special status, crime). ERO → TU (union representative). ERO → TES. ERO or LA → SAPS. INV → ERO (preliminary report).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Many weak cases are lost here: CCTV overwritten, a test result not properly recorded, or a manager’s “informal chat” that becomes the only account. Preserve first, interview second.

steps.title: Make safe
steps.trigger: Incident, allegation or complaint: theft, assault, intoxication, safety breach, harassment, dishonesty, absence.
steps.action: Stop the activity; separate the people involved; call security, medical help or SAPS where needed. Where an employee must leave the site at once (intoxication, violence), send them home on full pay for the rest of the shift and confirm in writing by the next working day. This is a same-day safety measure, not yet a suspension.

steps.trigger: Any manager learns of possible misconduct.
steps.action: Forward to the ERO the same day with the facts known, names, and where evidence sits. Do not interview the employee informally, promise an outcome or discuss it with the team.

steps.title: Criminal and reporting screen
steps.action: Decide on a SAPS report. A person in a position of authority who knows, ought reasonably to have known or suspects that an offence of corruption (PRECCA ss.3–16, 20–21), theft, fraud, extortion, forgery or uttering involving R100 000 or more has been committed must report it to a police official (DPCI); failing to report is itself an offence. Discipline need not wait for the criminal case; the tests and standard of proof differ.

steps.action: Move to the independent route: SSO or the Board chair appoints an external investigator and chair.

steps.trigger: Facts not clear or not admitted.
steps.action: Someone independent of the matter and of the future chair. Terms of reference: allegations, scope, preliminary report date, confidentiality, POPIA. External where senior management is implicated. Where the facts are clear and undisputed (an admitted absence, a confirmed test), record that no investigation is needed.

steps.action: Speak to the complainant and key witnesses; take first signed statements; collect the core documents; identify further evidence for Phase 3. steps.title: Route decision
steps.action: Choose: (a) no case — close and tell the employee in writing; (b) informal correction (item 6(6)); (c) expedited warning process, where a warning is the most severe possible outcome — a short-form version of Phases 4 and 5 without formal evidence-leading; (d) formal enquiry, where dismissal is possible — continue to Phase 3; (e) another process (incapacity, performance, probation, grievance). Check the precedent register.

steps.action: Calendar: suspension decision and reviews; evidence complete; notice served (with the 48-hour and two-working-day check); enquiry date; outcome letter; appeal; 30-day (restarted at any appeal outcome that upholds a dismissal) and 90-day referral windows; warning expiry dates.

stages.title: Phase 2 — Suspension decision and correspondence
intro: The suspension question is asked as soon as there is reasonable cause, often before the preliminary report is finished, and is revisited whenever circumstances change. Every step produces a letter: the paper trail is the employer’s only defence to an unfair suspension claim.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Make any representations honestly and on time; acknowledge receipt of letters; comply with the suspension conditions; remain contactable. A suspended employee remains an employee and still owes duties of good faith.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: ERO → SSO (sign-off). ERO → PAY and ITS (pay continues; access restricted). ERO → LM (team message). ERO → TU.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: A suspension without a stated reason, without pay, without a review date, or dragging on while nothing happens, can be an unfair labour practice even if the employee is later found guilty.

steps.title: Consider suspension
steps.trigger: Allegation of serious misconduct and a concern about the employee’s continued presence.
steps.action: ERO considers suspension on the facts then known and the investigator’s risk assessment. Line managers do not suspend without the ERO and SSO.
points: ERO considers suspension on the facts then known and the investigator’s risk assessment.
Line managers do not suspend without the ERO and SSO.
steps.deadline: As soon as reasonable cause exists

steps.title: Threshold test
steps.action: Suspend only if all three are met and recorded. (1) A reasonable belief, on the information available, that the employee committed serious misconduct. (2) An objectively justifiable reason to exclude them: risk of interfering with evidence or witnesses, of repeating the conduct, to safety or property, or a breakdown that makes continued presence untenable. (3) No less restrictive measure would do. Never use suspension to punish, pressure or “manage out”.

steps.title: Alternatives
steps.action: Consider restricted system or site access, temporary transfer on the same terms and pay, supervised duties, or a no-contact instruction. Record why each was accepted or rejected.

steps.title: Notice of intention to suspend
steps.action: Letter (or email with read receipt), in a language the employee understands: the allegation in general terms; why suspension is being considered; that it would be on full pay and is not a finding; an invitation to make written or oral representations, with a representative, by a stated time. Representations are a GBS policy safeguard; they are not a legal precondition after Long (CC 2019), so the employer must still record a fair reason (e.g. a reasonable apprehension of interference with the investigation or repetition of the conduct), and full pay limits the prejudice.

steps.action: Suspend at once by letter stating the reason, and invite representations within 48 hours; reconsider promptly and confirm, vary or lift in writing.

steps.title: Suspension letter

steps.action: Review whether the reason still exists and whether the matter is progressing; write to the employee confirming continuation (with reasons and the next review date), variation, or upliftment. stages.group: Phase 3 — Gathering evidence and the notice to attend
stages.title: Gathering evidence
intro: The employer bears the onus of proving the misconduct on a balance of probabilities, and of showing that dismissal, if imposed, was fair (s.192(2)). Evidence is gathered against each element of each charge, disclosed to the employee in time to prepare, and presented in Phase 4. The notice to attend is served only once the evidence is substantially complete.

steps.title: Evidence plan
steps.action: For each draft charge, list the elements to prove (rule, awareness, conduct, identity, time, place) and the evidence for each; identify gaps and who will obtain what by when.

stages.title: Phase 4 — The disciplinary enquiry
intro: The chairperson runs the enquiry in the order below and keeps a record throughout. The employer party (initiator) goes first because it bears the onus; the employee party always has the last word before each decision. Rulings on objections and procedural points are given with brief reasons on the record.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Attend or explain absence; conduct themselves properly; tell the truth; put their version to the employer’s witnesses; comply with procedural rulings.

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CHR → ERO (record and adjournment date). ERO → LA (if dismissal is likely). Scribe → CHR (record).

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: Two failures recur. An employee party that never put its version to a witness cannot fairly complain later that the witness was not challenged, and a chair who never explained that duty to an unrepresented employee risks a procedural finding. Explain it at 4.5 and remind the employee at 4.11.

steps.title: Welcome and introductions
steps.action: Chair introduces themselves and asks everyone present to state their name and role (employee, representative, initiator, interpreter, scribe, observers). Explains the purpose (to decide whether the employee is guilty and, if so, the appropriate sanction), that the chair has not decided anything in advance, that the proceedings are recorded, and the language to be used.

If any right was not met, the chair decides whether a short adjournment or postponement cures it.

stages.title: Phase 5 — Finding, mitigation, aggravation, sanction and outcome
intro: The finding on guilt and the sanction are separate decisions, each preceded by the parties’ submissions and each given with reasons. The employee party is heard on sanction before it is decided (item 11(4)(b)), even where the finding seems to make dismissal obvious.

notes.heading: Employee obligations at this stage
notes.text: Put any mitigation fully; return company property; lodge any appeal within the policy period; refer any dispute within 30 days (dismissal; from the appeal outcome if later) or 90 days (unfair labour practice).

notes.heading: Hand-offs
notes.text: CHR → ERO (outcome and reasons). ERO → PAY, HR and ITS (implementation). ERO → complainant. LA → CCMA or council.

notes.heading: Watch
notes.text: The 2025 Code no longer repeats the old Schedule 8 direction to give reasons and remind the employee of referral rights, but both remain good practice and remove later condonation arguments. If you offer an internal appeal, the 30-day period for a dismissal dispute runs from the appeal outcome; state this correctly in the outcome letter.

steps.action: For each charge decide: did a rule or standard exist; was it valid and reasonable; was the employee aware of it; did the employee contravene it (item 8(1)–(2)(b)). Where versions conflict, assess each witness’s credibility, the reliability of their evidence, and the probabilities, and say which version is more probable and why.

intro: Every report feeds one intake. Phase 1 ends with the route decision; only matters where dismissal is a possible outcome go through the full enquiry. referenceTables.section: §15 Corrections to existing GBS materials and drafting issues
rows: The company “complies with the requirements set out in Schedule 8 of the Labour Relations Act (Code of Good Practice on Dismissal)”
Schedule 8 was repealed on 4 September 2025. Cite the Code of Good Practice: Dismissal, 2025 (GN 3470, GG 53294), items 6 to 13 for misconduct.
“Minimum notice period: 1 working day before the hearing”
§5.5; §8.4 Step 2; Appendix B para 1; Appendix D Q1

Replace with the rule in this flow: at least 48 hours from proven service, including at least two full working days, and longer (BP 5 working days) for complex matters. Item 11(4)(b) requires a reasonable period to prepare; one working day will seldom meet it where dismissal is possible.
Line managers may issue up to a final written warning on the same day; no written notice to attend for warnings

Defensible for informal correction and verbal or written warnings where the employee knows the allegation and evidence and genuinely responds (items 6(6), 11(3)). A final written warning is disciplinary action that can be challenged under s.186(2)(b) and may later support dismissal: require at least a short written notice and time to arrange a representative.
Expired warnings “can be used as evidence of previous disciplinary history (aggravation)” and “remain on file”
§2.10; §8.4 Step 4(h); §11.4; Appendix A notes; Appendix D

Relying on expired warnings to escalate a sanction undermines the validity periods the code itself sets and is widely treated as unfair. Remove the statement, or confine any use to showing awareness of a rule, on LA advice (CL, verify). Keep the record for retention purposes only.
Suspension clause of six lines; one suspension paragraph in the notice

Add the threshold test, representations, the six letters in the Phase 2 correspondence register (forms D11 to D15, with D12 in standard and urgent variants), full pay, 30-day reviews, access to prepare a defence, upliftment, union notice, and the distinction from unpaid suspension as a sanction.
Enquiry order: company’s case, then employee’s case; finding; mitigation and aggravation

Align with Phase 4: add confirmation of preliminary rights, opening statements, re-examination, chair’s questions, a no-case application, closing statements, and the order for sanction submissions (employer aggravation, then employee mitigation, employee last word). Explain the duty to put one’s version to witnesses.
Refusing a breathalyser or drug test: “presumption of guilt”
Appendix A, Alcohol and Drug Offences

Refusal can be separate misconduct (refusing a lawful and reasonable instruction under a communicated testing policy), but it does not create a presumption of intoxication. Reword and charge refusal separately.

“Dismissal” as the sanction for a first offence in categories with a wide range of seriousness (inappropriate social media posts; all POPIA processing failures; “failure to obtain proper consent”; unauthorised use of own systems; possession of cannabis on premises)

Items 8(2)(f) and 9 require the sanction to fit the case. Write “up to dismissal”, or split categories by seriousness, and state that the table guides and does not decide. Check the cannabis entries against Prince (CC 2018), the Cannabis for Private Purposes Act 7 of 2024 (commencement, verify) and Enever v Barloworld Equipment [2024] ZALAC 12 (zero-tolerance cannabis policy without evidence of impairment held unfair); frame cannabis rules around impairment and safety-critical roles, not positive tests alone.
Absence of 3 or more consecutive days: dismissal
Distinguish absence (misconduct) from desertion (an intention not to return) and from illness (incapacity). Require documented attempts to contact the employee before any enquiry in absence.
Right to an interpreter “for potential dismissal matters”
Item 11(4)(d) is not limited to dismissal: give the opportunity to converse in a language the employee is comfortable with, where reasonably possible, including in the expedited process.

Add a discretion clause: normally a fellow employee or union representative (item 11(4)(c)); the chair may allow legal representation in complex or serious matters (CL: MEC Finance, Northern Province v Mahumani (SCA 2004); Dorkin (LAC 2008), verify).
Referral right stated only as “CCMA within 30 days if dismissed”

Add referral to a bargaining council where one has jurisdiction; unfair labour practice disputes (including suspensions and warnings) within 90 days; automatically unfair dismissals to the Labour Court after conciliation; condonation; and that, where an internal appeal is offered, the 30-day period for a dismissal dispute runs from the appeal outcome (s.191(1)(b)(i)); an internal appeal does not extend the 90-day unfair labour practice period. See step 5.10.
Enquiries “will proceed” in the employee’s absence

Only after proper service and reasonable attempts to contact; the chair considers any explanation and may postpone once (Code items 11(2), 11(4)(b); BP; CL). Item 11(6) is the separate exceptional-circumstances exemption and is not relied on here.
“Minimal record-keeping for warnings and final warnings”
Item 13 requires records of the nature of the transgression, the action taken and the reasons. Keep warning records brief but complete.
Evidence mentioned only generally (“Manager gathers relevant evidence”)
Add the evidence plan, chain of custody, the lawfulness check and disclosure of the bundle with the notice (steps 3.1 to 3.8 and the types-of-evidence table).
Demotion and transfer only with written agreement; no unpaid suspension option

Decide, with LA, whether the code should permit demotion or unpaid suspension as alternatives to dismissal where dismissal would otherwise be justified (verify). Where offered, record the employee’s election.
Harassment listed only as a dismissal offence
Cross-refer the Code of Good Practice on the Prevention and Elimination of Harassment in the Workplace (GN R.1890, GG 46056, 18 March 2022; EEA s.54) and add the complainant-protection steps in P8.
Consent is not the only lawful basis under POPIA s.11(1); recording on notice for an accurate record is defensible. Announce recordings and keep them secure.
Probation and TES workers not addressed
Add pointers: probation (items 14 to 18, including representations before dismissal or extension) and TES workers (the TES is the employer, s.198(2); the client reports and requests removal).

intro: The notice is headed “Code of Practice: Dismissal” and the text “Code of Good Practice: Dismissal”, and the Code is itself headed “Schedule 8” although the notice says its publication repeals Schedule 8. It is unclear whether it takes Schedule 8’s place in the Act or stands alone. Cite it by notice and Gazette number.

The notice gives s.203(2A) of the LRA (a code issued by the Minister after consideration by NEDLAC) as the power under which the Code was issued; this was confirmed against the notice text on Acts Online in October 2026. The January 2025 draft cited s.203(2), so cite the final notice, not the draft.

The Code is silent on precautionary suspension, although footnote 2 lists “suspension” among graduated disciplinary measures. This invites confusion between a precautionary suspension on full pay and unpaid suspension as a sanction.
It sets no minimum notice period and no order of proceedings, leaving both to “a reasonable period of time to prepare” (item 11(4)(b)) and internal policy.
It gives no guidance on warning validity periods or on the use of expired warnings.
Item 11 is framed around a decision to dismiss and says nothing about the procedure for warnings, although s.186(2)(b) makes unfair disciplinary action short of dismissal an unfair labour practice.
The old Schedule 8 direction to give the employee the reason for dismissal and remind them of the right to refer a dispute has not been carried over.
Item 11(4)(c) mentions only a fellow employee or union representative; it is silent on legal representation and on reasonable accommodation for employees with disabilities.
Item 7(1) defines a fair reason for misconduct dismissal by reference to intolerability, which is also the sanction test in item 9; the reason and sanction questions are blurred.
Item 3 does not define a small business.
